clue.text: Piece of tiling on church blokes fix

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed on another follows it, so what comes before this word in the clue goes after in the answer

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
blokes are men

indicators.note: a piece is only a small part of something, so just one letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Workmen at a church are mending a bit of broken tiling.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means placed after, so the tiling letter goes at the end, behind the church and the blokes.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement something is to bind it firmly in place, just as you would fix it.

clue.text: Broadcast channel lacking in refinement

indicators.note: a broadcast goes out over the air to be heard, so we want a word that sounds like another

parts.note: a channel for water is a course, as in watercourse

explanation.surface: A TV station is criticised for crude, unsophisticated programming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast channel' reads as a TV station, but the channel is the path a stream runs in, and broadcast says we only hear it.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse manners or language are rough and vulgar, the opposite of polished or cultivated.

clue.text: Police squad coming up with no answer

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means reading from the bottom to the top
having none of something means it has been taken away

parts.note: a squad is a team
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A police unit arrives on the scene but has no answers for anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police squad' looks like one unit, but only the first word is the definition. The Met is London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: The Met is the everyday short name for London's Metropolitan Police force.

clue.text: Commentary about a bishop's state

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the others

parts.note: a state is a nation
RR stands for Right Reverend, a bishop's title
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is commenting on how a bishop's diocese is getting on.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is not possessive: it is 'is', so the bishop sits in the state. The pair goes in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A narration is a spoken account accompanying film or events, which is what a commentary provides.

clue.text: Disorderly struggle in anagrammatic game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a frantic scramble or grab for something
second meaning: the board game of building words from letter tiles

explanation.surface: Players come to blows during a heated board game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anagrammatic' tempts you to look for an anagram, but it simply describes the game, where letters are rearranged into words.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a messy scrambling contest and is also the name of the popular tile-based word game.

clue.text: Criminal and female do drugs to get dizzy

parts.note: a con is a convict
F is the abbreviation for female
to use is slang for taking drugs

explanation.surface: A crook and his girlfriend take drugs and end up light-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dizzy' reads as an adjective, but here it is the verb: to make someone dizzy.
explanation.definitionFit: To dizzy someone is to bewilder them, leaving their head spinning, which is what confusing does.

clue.text: Creative works describing old atomic vessel

indicators.note: to describe is also to draw a line round something, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: art is creative work
O is the abbreviation for old
A stands for atomic, as in A-bomb

explanation.surface: Artworks depict a vintage nuclear-powered ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship after 'atomic', but it is a blood vessel. Describing is used in its geometric sense of drawing round.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorta is the main artery leaving the heart, the largest blood vessel in the body.

clue.text: Atrocious teller being argumentative

indicators.note: something atrocious is terribly done, so the letters come out badly jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dreadful bank clerk picks quarrels with the customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' looks like a link word but its letters are needed: the fodder is both words together.
explanation.definitionFit: Belligerent describes someone hostile and eager to fight or quarrel, a stronger synonym for argumentative.

clue.text: Changed, and hence, made better

indicators.note: changed means altered, so the order of the letters is altered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something was altered, and as a result improved.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the clue so 'and hence' reads as logic, but those two words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance is to improve quality or value, so something enhanced has been improved.

clue.text: Dogs in underwear

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a breed of square-jawed dog
second meaning: loose men's shorts worn as underpants

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures pets dressed in pants; the two nouns are separate meanings of one plural word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a muscular dog breed and also the loose shorts men wear beneath trousers.

clue.text: Post given to short nob regarding PM

indicators.note: something short has been cut, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: post means after, as in post-war
the word NOB with its last letter cut off, as 'short' instructs
on means about or regarding

explanation.surface: A job is handed to a diminutive toff in connection with the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PM' looks like the Prime Minister, but it is post meridiem, the time after noon. A nob is British slang for a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: PM, from the Latin post meridiem, marks the hours after midday, the second half of the day.

clue.text: Charge husband assuming Latin man's name

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so one piece takes in another

parts.note: a rap is a criminal charge
L is the abbreviation for Latin
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A married man is accused of using a false Latin name.
explanation.walkthrough: The husband comes last, after the charge has taken in its letter, although he is named first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph is an ordinary male first name, so it is an example of what the clue asks for.

clue.text: Group of soldiers holding large American dance

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: the SAS is the Special Air Service regiment
L is the abbreviation for large
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A platoon puts on a big American dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American dance' wants to be the definition, but American gives a letter and the dance stands alone. The SAS is a British special forces regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Salsa is a lively Latin American partner dance, so it is one example of the category.

clue.text: Machine that could ruin pork pie merchant?

definitions.text: Machine that could ruin pork pie merchant?

parts.words: Machine that could ruin pork pie merchant?
parts.note: surface reading: some device that might put a pie seller out of business
setter's reading: pork pie is rhyming slang for an untruth, so a pork pie merchant is a habitual fibber, whom this machine exposes

explanation.walkthrough: Pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie, so the merchant deals in falsehoods, not pastry; a polygraph would ruin such a dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: A polygraph measures pulse and breathing to expose falsehoods, which would finish the career of a practised fibber.

clue.text: A cute don I fooled around with gives you this

definitions.text: A cute don I fooled around with gives you this

indicators.note: fooling around is messing about, so the letters are messed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that a fling with an attractive university lecturer taught them a thing or two.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a don is a university teacher, and what dons give you is learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A don teaches students at a university, so schooling and learning are what one provides.

clue.text: Careless soldiers fail to hit target

parts.note: the RE are the Royal Engineers
to miss is to fail to hit

explanation.surface: Sloppy troops keep missing at the firing range.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers are a British Army corps, a stock source of these two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Remiss describes someone negligent in their duty, which is a formal way of calling them careless.

clue.text: Intense old flame very short with Hoskins

indicators.note: something short has been cut, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a former partner is an ex
very in French is TRES, cut short
Hoskins is the setter, who refers to themself

explanation.surface: A former lover had a brief, passionate fling with the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, so his name stands for the setter speaking. 'Very' becomes French before being cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something of great strength or degree, far beyond the ordinary level.

clue.text: Fresh Argentine fruit

indicators.note: something fresh is newly made, so the letters are made into a new word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Produce newly imported from Argentina is on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' reads naturally with fruit, but it is the instruction to rework the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small, loose-skinned citrus like a mandarin, one kind of fruit.

clue.text: Concerning to have sex and strain yourself?

parts.note: over can mean about, as in a row over money
to do it is a euphemism for having sex

explanation.surface: Someone worries that sex might leave them pulling a muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' looks like worrying, but it is the preposition meaning about.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdo it is an idiom for working too hard or pushing beyond your limits.

clue.text: Compete with Tesla guy over land

parts.note: to vie is to compete
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a guy is a man

explanation.surface: A rival tries to beat the electric car boss in a battle for territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tesla guy' points at the car company's boss, but Tesla is the physics unit and the guy is a separate piece. 'Over land' reads as flying; over turns the guy round.
explanation.definitionFit: Vietnam is a country in Southeast Asia, and a country is a land.

clue.text: Old lady seen with a bloke in the shade?

parts.note: one's old lady is one's mother, ma
a gent is a man
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grandmother is spotted sitting out of the sun with a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the shade' suggests shelter from the sun, but the shade is a colour. The single letter goes after the bloke.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red colour, and a shade is a particular tint or hue.

clue.text: Brown river in Scottish city

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish brown
the Dee is a river in Scotland

explanation.surface: A muddy river runs through a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' tempts you to put one piece inside another, but it only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dundee is a city on the Firth of Tay on Scotland's east coast.

clue.text: Give smack up during party with junkie at last

indicators.note: something happening during something else sits within it

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to tan someone is to give them a beating

indicators.note: the very end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to hand over heroin at a party where an addict has finally shown up.
explanation.walkthrough: Smack looks like heroin beside 'junkie', but it is a beating. The turned word goes inside the party plus the junkie's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to give money or goods as a gift, usually to a cause.

clue.text: Aristocrat reportedly unable to produce heir?

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so we hear a word rather than read it

parts.note: a baron is a nobleman

explanation.surface: Gossip says a nobleman cannot father a successor.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that heir is a playful way of saying offspring, fitting the noble theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Barren means infertile, unable to have children, so no heir could be born.

clue.text: Learner finally gets grade one playing this?

definitions.text: Learner finally gets grade one playing this?

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of a word

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

indicators.note: playing with something moves it around, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A music student passes a first-grade exam on some keyboard instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a beginner who has passed grade one could be playing this instrument. 'Learner' is not L here; only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed organ, such as a harmonium, is a keyboard instrument a pupil might sit exams on.

clue.text: Love wicked character written by Aristophanes

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, written as O
wicked and mega are both slang for excellent

explanation.surface: Someone adores a villain from one of Aristophanes' comedies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a role in a play, but it is a letter of the alphabet, one Aristophanes would have used writing in Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, so the Athenian playwright wrote it.

clue.text: Drug given to cross flipping Art actor with no lines?

parts.note: E is ecstasy
a cross is the letter X

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cross, swearing actor in the play Art is given drugs to calm him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild swearword, and Art as the stage play, but it simply turns the word round.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra appears in the background of a film or play without speaking any part.

clue.text: Blooming half-cut Reed is unconventional

indicators.note: cutting something in half keeps only one part, so half the letters go

parts.note: flowers that are blooming are out
the word with its second half cut away

explanation.surface: A tipsy Reed behaves outlandishly; half-cut is British slang for drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like a mild curse and half-cut like drunk, but they are flowering and half the letters removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré, borrowed from French, describes something bizarre or beyond the bounds of convention.

clue.text: Drunkenly inept Rick is overly-fussy critic

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of order, so the letters lurch into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Clumsy, tipsy Rick is a pedantic reviewer.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the two words after the indicator, and the definition is the long phrase at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitpicker finds fault with tiny trivial details, the idiom for a pedantic person who complains too much.

clue.text: Equipment used in ASK Italian

indicators.note: what is used in something is found inside it, so the letters sit within the words

parts.note: spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Kitchen gear used at a restaurant of the ASK Italian chain.
explanation.walkthrough: ASK Italian is a British chain of Italian restaurants; the capitals make it look like a brand, which it is, but its letters hold the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Kit is the everyday British word for the gear or apparatus needed for a particular activity.

clue.text: Refuse entry to performer on vacation

parts.note: a turn is a performer's act, as in a music-hall turn
on holiday you are away

explanation.surface: A bouncer stops an entertainer on holiday from getting in.
explanation.walkthrough: A turn is British for a performer or act on a variety bill; 'Refuse entry to' needs its object, so the preposition stays in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn someone away is the idiom for not admitting them at the door.

clue.text: Mostly endure down-a-man side getting thrashed

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is lost

parts.note: to bear is to endure, cut short
a football or cricket side has eleven players, so one man down leaves ten

explanation.surface: A team reduced to ten players hangs on but is soundly defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated phrase is one piece: a side a man down is a number, not a team.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrashed can mean heavily defeated or physically struck, and beaten carries both senses.
